passages.text:
The following text is from an original short story.
Marisol had expected the abandoned greenhouse to be empty, but it was ______ with life: ferns crowded every bench, and vines had climbed all the way to the cracked glass roof.

passages.title: Foundations
passages.text: Bridges are usually admired for their spans, the distances between their supports. Engineer Tomás Reyes, however, argues that the most important part of a bridge is the part no one sees: its foundation. "A long span on a weak foundation," he says, "is simply a dramatic way to fail."
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Repair café
passages.text: Once a month, a community center in the town of Alder Creek hosts a "repair café," where volunteers fix residents' broken lamps, toasters, and bicycles for free. Organizers say the event keeps hundreds of items out of the landfill each year. Just as important, they add, residents who watch the repairs often learn to fix similar problems on their own.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Feeder survey
passages.text:
A student counted the birds visiting three feeders in her yard over four weeks. Each feeder held a different food.
Feeder | Food | Total visits
1 | Sunflower seeds | 212
2 | Thistle seeds | 87
3 | Suet | 145
The student concluded that, of the three foods, sunflower seeds attracted the most visits.

passages.text:

• Glass bottles and plastic bottles can both be recycled.

• Recycled glass is often used to make new bottles.

passages.title: Tardigrades
passages.text: For years, many biologists assumed that tardigrades, tiny animals that can survive being almost completely dried out, protected themselves mainly by producing a sugar called trehalose, which helps shield cells in some other organisms. Yet when researchers measured trehalose in several tardigrade species, they found little or none. Further work identified proteins found only in tardigrades that form a glass-like gel as the animals dry, apparently protecting their cells until water returns.

passages.title: Learning words (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Some teachers argue that the fastest way for students to build vocabulary is to memorize lists of words and their definitions. Students can review dozens of words in a single sitting, and quiz scores often rise within days.

Text 2
Researchers who study reading point out that definitions memorized for a quiz are often forgotten within weeks. Words met repeatedly in meaningful reading, by contrast, tend to be retained, because readers see how the words are actually used.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Shell chains
passages.text: Marine biologists have observed that when an empty shell larger than any in a group appears, hermit crabs nearby often line up by size beside it. When the largest crab moves into the new shell, the next crab in line takes the shell it left behind, and so on down the line. This pattern suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Historian
passages.text: Unlike earlier accounts of the mill town's decline, which blamed a single cause, the historian's new study is notably ______: she weighs several possible explanations and openly acknowledges the limits of the surviving records.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Highway lanes (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Some transportation planners argue that adding lanes to a congested highway reduces traffic. As evidence, they point to a widening project after which average travel times on the highway fell during the following year.

Text 2
Researchers who study "induced demand" report that when lanes are added to congested highways, travel times often improve at first, but within a few years the new lanes tend to fill as more people choose to drive, and congestion returns to roughly its earlier level.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.text:

Town | Visits in 2019 | Visits in 2023
A | 12,000 | 15,000
B | 30,000 | 34,500
C | 8,000 | 10,400
The researcher noted that the town with the largest percentage increase in visits was not the town with the largest increase in the number of visits.

passages.text: Divers spent three seasons excavating a merchant ship that sank off the coast more than two thousand years ago. passages.title: Songbird migration notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A researcher tracked two populations of a migratory songbird.
• One population nests in Norway; the other nests in Spain.
• Both populations spend the winter in West Africa.
• The Norwegian birds left West Africa an average of 9 days earlier than the Spanish birds.
• The Norwegian birds reached their nesting grounds an average of 11 days later than the Spanish birds.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Marsh grazing
passages.text: In one salt marsh, ecologists fenced snails out of some plots of cordgrass and left other plots open. After a season, the fenced plots held dense cordgrass, while many open plots had been grazed bare. In a nearby marsh where snail-eating crabs are abundant, however, the open plots looked nearly identical to the fenced ones. These results suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Songbird pitch
passages.text: Ecologist Dara Mensah studies a songbird whose city populations sing at a higher pitch than its rural populations. Many researchers attribute the difference to traffic noise, which masks low-pitched sounds. Mensah instead hypothesizes that young birds simply learn the songs of the adults around them, and that the first birds to settle in the city happened to sing at a higher pitch.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Late quartets
passages.text: Composer Lena Ostrova's early string quartets were praised for their dense counterpoint, with all four instruments carrying independent melodies at once. Her later quartets abandon that density, often giving a single melody to one instrument while the others hold long, quiet chords. Some critics have called this change a decline in ambition. Ostrova's sketchbooks, however, show that she revised these sparse passages more times than any of her earlier music.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Committee report
passages.text: Although the committee's final report ran to more than two hundred pages, its recommendations were notably ______: each could be carried out within a single budget year by the city's existing staff.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Crater streaks
passages.text: For years, dark streaks that appear on the walls of certain Martian craters were widely thought to be traces of flowing salty water. When planetary scientist Teodor Lind compared the streaks' locations with maps of slope, however, he found that they occur only on slopes steep enough for dry sand and dust to slide on their own. Lind argues that the streaks are better explained as small avalanches of dry material.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Four-day week (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Economist Rosa Iglesias argues that a four-day workweek raises productivity. She points to a group of firms where output per hour rose after employees switched to working four days a week.

Text 2
Labor researchers note that the firms volunteering for four-day-week trials tend to be ones whose managers already expect the change to succeed and whose work can easily be compressed into fewer days. Results from such firms, the researchers caution, may not hold for workplaces in general.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.text:
A researcher measured the percentage of seeds that germinated for two wildflower species at three soil temperatures.
Soil temperature | Species X | Species Y
10°C | 12% | 40%
18°C | 55% | 62%
26°C | 81% | 58%
The researcher claims that Species X's germination is more sensitive to soil temperature than Species Y's is.

Herders who raise animals mainly for meat tend to slaughter them young, whatever their sex, whereas herders who keep animals for milk tend to keep females into adulthood and cull most young males. The pattern in the village therefore suggests that ______

passages.title: Covered market
passages.text: Many visitors to the old covered market in Varos assume that its maze of alleys grew without any plan. Historian Selin Aydın's study of property records complicates that view. The market's oldest section, she found, was laid out on a deliberate grid around two stone storehouses; only the later additions, built as trade expanded, wandered outward along whatever streets already existed.

passages.title: Cholera map
passages.text: In the 1850s, many physicians in London held that cholera spread through foul air. During an 1854 outbreak, physician John Snow mapped the homes of those who died and found that they clustered around a single public water pump. Workers at a nearby brewery, who drank the beer they were given rather than water from the pump, were largely spared. Snow's findings pointed to contaminated water, not air, as the source.

passages.title: The letter
passages.text:
The following text is from a short story. Mrs. Hale has just received a letter.
She read the letter twice, the second time more slowly, as though the words might rearrange themselves into something kinder if given the opportunity. They did not. She folded it along its creases, laid it upon the mantel beside the clock, and turned to the window, where the afternoon was going about its business with a composure she could not help resenting.

But because the second group consists entirely of people who chose not to buy, the difference may instead reflect the fact that ______

• It had remained unsolved for 70 years.
• Okonjo's proof uses a technique from probability theory.

passages.title: Printing press
passages.text: Many historians have argued that the printing press spread quickly across Europe because it dramatically lowered the cost of books. Historian Imre Halasz agrees that printing eventually made books cheaper, but he notes that in the first decades after its introduction, printed books often sold for about as much as manuscripts did. He also observes that the earliest presses clustered in cities that already had universities and established book trades.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Cat domestication
passages.text: Early accounts portrayed the domestication of cats as deliberate: people, it was said, tamed wild cats to protect stored grain from rodents. Genetic studies have complicated this picture. Domestic cats show far fewer genetic differences from their wild ancestors than domestic dogs do from theirs, and those differences arose gradually over thousands of years. Some researchers now argue that cats largely domesticated themselves, tolerating people in exchange for easy access to prey, long before humans took any deliberate role in their breeding.

• Composer Daniel Oyelaran wrote the opera Harbor Lights (2004).
• Salt Road is set in a nineteenth-century mining town; Harbor Lights is set in a modern port city.

passages.title: Night heat
passages.text: Most studies of urban heat have focused on daytime temperatures. Yet for human health, nighttime temperatures may matter more, because the body recovers from daytime heat stress only when temperatures fall after dark. Climatologist Kofi Asante's measurements show that in dense neighborhoods, pavement and buildings release stored heat at night, keeping nights as much as 5°C warmer than in nearby parks.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Salmon decline
passages.text: For decades, the decline of salmon in the Varna River was blamed on overfishing. When fishing limits were tightened in the 1990s, however, salmon numbers kept falling. Biologist Mara Lindqvist then noticed that the decline closely tracked the construction of small dams on the river's tributaries, which block salmon from reaching their spawning streams. Since several of those dams were removed in 2015, salmon counts in the affected tributaries have tripled.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.text:
The following text is from a short story. Inés has recently moved from her grandmother's rural home to a city apartment.
At night the building was never quiet. Pipes knocked in the walls, a neighbor's television murmured through the floor, and the elevator groaned between stories. Inés had expected to find the noise unbearable. Instead, lying awake on the third night, she realized she had been listening for it, the way she had once listened for the creek behind her grandmother's house.

passages.title: Irrigation yields
passages.text:

Crop | Without irrigation | With irrigation

passages.text:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Teodora has returned to her childhood village after twenty years away.

passages.text:

For weeks Ana's scales sounded like a door creaking in the wind. She practiced them anyway, every evening, while her brother complained through the wall. It had simply rung, clear and round, and for a moment she was afraid to play the next one in case it would not.
